title: Cleomedes and the chest
source_text: Ἔδειξε δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι πλείονας ἀνέγνω ἱστορίας Ἑλληνικὰς, παραθέμενος καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἀστυπαλαιέως Κλεομήδους· ὃν ἱστόρησεν εἰς κιβωτὸν καταδύντα καὶ ἔνδοθεν αὐτῆς εἰλημμένον μὴ εὑρῆσθαι ἔνδον· ἀλλ᾿ ἔκτοθι δαιμονίᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ διαπτῆναι, ἡνίκα ὑπὲρ τοῦ αὐτὸν συλλαβεῖν διέκοψάν τινες τὴν κιβωτόν. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ εἰ μὲν πλάσμα ἐστὶν, ὥσπερ ἔοικεν εἶναι πλάσμα, οὐ παραβάλλεται τοῖς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ· ἐπείπερ ἐκείνων μὲν οὐδὲν τῆς ἱστορουμένης θειότητος ἐν τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σύμβολον εὑρίσκεται, τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ αἱ τῶν ὠφελουμένων ἐκκλησίαι καὶ αἱ περὶ αὐτοῦ λελεγμέναι προφητεῖαι καὶ αἱ ἐν ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ γινόμεναι θεραπεῖαι καὶ ἡ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν μετὰ σοφίας γνῶσις καὶ λόγος εὑρισκόμενος παρὰ τοῖς φροντίσασιν ἀναβῆναι μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ψιλῆς πίστεως, ἐρευνῆσαι δὲ τὸν ἐν ταῖς θείαις γραφαῖς νοῦν κατὰ τὰς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὑποθήκας εἰπόντος· „ἐρευνᾶτε τὰς γραφὰς,“ καὶ κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ διδάξαντος Παύλου δεῖν „εἰδέναι“ ἡμᾶς „ἑκάστῳ“ κατὰ τὸ δέον „ἀποκρίνεσθαι.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ εἰπόντος· „ἕτοιμοι ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι ὑμᾶς λόγον περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν πίστεως.“ εἰ δὲ βούλεται αὐτὸς συγχωρεῖσθαι μὴ εἶναι πλάσμα. λεγέτω. τί βουλομένη ἡ ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον δύναμις πεποίηκεν ἔκτοθι τῆς κιβωτοῦ δαιμονίᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ διαπτῆναι. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἀξιόλογόν τι παραστήσει καὶ βούλημα θεοῦ ἄξιον τὸ δωρησάμενον τὸ τοιοῦτον τῷ Κλεομήδει, κρινοῦμεν, τί χρὴ λέγειν πρὸς αὐτόν· εἰ δ᾿ ἀπορήσει κἂν πιθανόν τι εἰς τὸν τόπον λέγειν. δηλονότι τὸ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ εὑρίσκεσθαι λόγον, ἤτοι διαβαλοῦμεν τοῖς αὐτὴν μὴ παραδεξαμένοις καὶ ἐγκαλέσομεν τῇ ἱστορίᾳ ὡς οὐκ ἀληθεῖ, ἢ δαιμόνιόν τι φήσομεν παραπλήσιον τοῖς ἐπιδεικνυμένοις γόησιν ἀπάτῃ ὀφθαλμῶν πεποιηκέναι καὶ περὶ τὸν Ἀστυπαλαιέα· περὶ οὗ οἴεται ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι θεοπρόπιόν τι ἐθέσπισεν. ὡς ἄρα μοίρᾳ τινὶ δαιμονίᾳ διέπτη ἀπὸ τῆς κιβωτοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: And Celsus showed that he had read (ἀναγινώσκω) more Greek stories (ἱστορίαι Ἑλληνικαί), having set forth (παρατίθημι) also the things about Cleomedes the Astypalaean; whom he related (ἱστορέω) having got down into (καταδύω) a chest (κιβωτός) and, having been shut in (λαμβάνω, εἰλημμένον) from inside it, not to have been found (εὑρίσκω) inside, but outside (ἔκτοθι) by some demonic/supernatural lot (δαιμονίᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ) to have flown through/out (διαπέτομαι), when for the sake of seizing (συλλαμβάνω) him some cut through/broke (διακόπτω) the chest. And this, if it is a fiction (πλάσμα), as it seems to be a fiction, is not compared (παραβάλλω) with the things about Jesus; since of those no token (σύμβολον) of the reported (ἱστορέω) divinity (θειότης) is found in the life of men, but of Jesus the churches (ἐκκλησίαι) of those benefited (ὠφελέω), and the prophecies (προφητεῖαι) spoken about him, and the healings (θεραπεῖαι) happening in his name (ὄνομα), and the knowledge (γνῶσις) according to him with wisdom (σοφία) and reason/account (λόγος) found among those who took care (φροντίζω) to go up (ἀναβαίνω) from bare faith (ψιλὴ πίστις), and to search (ἐρευνάω) the meaning (νοῦς) in the divine writings (θεῖαι γραφαί) according to the counsels (ὑποθῆκαι) of Jesus who said: search the Scriptures; and according to the will (βούλημα) of Paul who taught that we must know to answer (ἀποκρίνομαι) each one as is needful (κατὰ τὸ δέον); but also of him who said: ready (ἕτοιμοι) always for defence (ἀπολογία) to everyone asking you a reason (λόγος) about the faith (πίστις) in you. But if he himself wishes it granted not to be a fiction, let him say: wishing what (τί βουλομένη) the power above man (ἡ ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον δύναμις) made [him] outside the chest by some demonic lot fly out. For if he presents (παρίστημι) something noteworthy (ἀξιόλογον) and a purpose worthy of God as that which bestowed (δωρέομαι) such a thing on Cleomedes, we shall judge (κρίνω) what one must say to him; but if he is at a loss (ἀπορέω) even to say something plausible (πιθανόν) on the topic (τόπος), clearly, so far as regards a reason not being found, we shall either discredit (διαβάλλω) [it] with those who did not accept (παραδέχομαι) it and accuse (ἐγκαλέω) the story as not true, or we shall say that something demonic (δαιμόνιόν τι), like to those displaying (ἐπιδείκνυμι) to sorcerers (γόητες) by deceit of eyes (ἀπάτη ὀφθαλμῶν), acted (ποιέω) also around the Astypalaean; about whom Celsus thinks that some oracle (θεοπρόπιον) prophesied (θεσπίζω) that then by some demonic lot he flew out from the chest.
pass_b_english: Celsus showed that he had read a good many Greek stories when he also cited the tale of Cleomedes of Astypalaea. He related that Cleomedes got into a chest and, though shut inside it, was not found within, but by some supernatural fate had flown out of it, when some men broke the chest open to seize him. If this too is a fiction, as it seems to be, it cannot be compared with the accounts of Jesus. For in the case of those men no token of the divinity reported of them is found in the life of men; but in the case of Jesus there are the churches of those who are helped, the prophecies spoken about him, the healings done in his name, and the knowledge joined with wisdom that comes from him, and the reasoned understanding found among those who have taken care to rise above bare faith and to search out the meaning in the divine Scriptures. They do this following the counsel of Jesus, who said, “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39), and the wish of Paul, who taught that we must “know how to answer each one” as is fitting (Colossians 4:6), and of him also who said, “Always be ready to make a defence to everyone who asks you for a reason for the faith that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15).

But if Celsus wants it granted that the story is not a fiction, let him say for what purpose the power that is above man made Cleomedes fly out of the chest by some supernatural fate. For if he can present something worth mentioning, and show that a purpose worthy of God bestowed such a thing on Cleomedes, we shall judge what we ought to say in reply to him. But if he is at a loss to say anything even plausible on the point, then plainly, so far as no reason is to be found, we shall either discredit the story, siding with those who did not accept it, and charge it with being untrue, or we shall say that something demonic, like the illusions that sorcerers display by deceiving the eyes, did this also in the case of the man from Astypalaea, about whom Celsus supposes that an oracle declared that he had flown out of the chest by some supernatural fate.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 33 (Koetschau 3.33). Celsus’s Cleomedes tale is reported in indirect speech (accusative and infinitive after ἱστόρησεν) and is left without quotation marks; the closing clause about the oracle is likewise indirect (οἴεται … ὅτι … ἐθέσπισεν). The legend is told also by Pausanias 6.9.6–8 and Plutarch, Romulus 28; not cited inline because Origen is answering Celsus, not quoting them. ‘δαιμονίᾳ τινὶ μοίρᾳ’ is Celsus’s phrase (repeated by Origen ironically) and is rendered ‘by some supernatural fate’: in Celsus’s mouth δαιμόνιος means ‘divine, marvellous’, not ‘demonic’; when Origen speaks for himself later (‘δαιμόνιόν τι … πεποιηκέναι’) it is rendered ‘something demonic’. ‘εἰλημμένον ἔνδοθεν’ rendered ‘shut inside it’ (literally ‘caught from within’). ‘ἀναβῆναι μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ψιλῆς πίστεως’ rendered ‘rise above bare faith’ (literally ‘go up from’). ‘ἐρευνᾶτε τὰς γραφάς’ = John 5:39. Paul’s phrase ‘εἰδέναι … ἑκάστῳ … ἀποκρίνεσθαι’ = Colossians 4:6 (εἰδέναι πῶς δεῖ ὑμᾶς ἑνὶ ἑκάστῳ ἀποκρίνεσθαι). The last quotation is 1 Peter 3:15, but Origen’s text reads ‘περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν πίστεως’ (the faith in you) where the received text of 1 Peter has ‘ἐλπίδος’ (the hope in you); translated as Origen gives it. ‘τοῦ εἰπόντος’ (him who said) is left unnamed, as in the Greek (Peter). ‘διαβαλοῦμεν τοῖς αὐτὴν μὴ παραδεξαμένοις’ is doubtful: the dative could mean ‘discredit it before those who have not accepted it’ or ‘discredit it along with those who did not accept it’; the second is followed (‘siding with those who did not accept it’), since Origen is listing his own two possible responses. ‘παραπλήσιον τοῖς ἐπιδεικνυμένοις γόησιν ἀπάτῃ ὀφθαλμῶν’: τοῖς ἐπιδεικνυμένοις is taken as neuter passive (the things displayed), γόησιν as dative of agent and ἀπάτῃ ὀφθαλμῶν as means; rendered ‘like the illusions that sorcerers display by deceiving the eyes’. ‘βούλημα θεοῦ ἄξιον τὸ δωρησάμενον’ rendered ‘show that a purpose worthy of God bestowed’ (the participle is predicative to βούλημα).

Stiff ‘a purpose worthy of God, as what bestowed’ made ‘show that a purpose worthy of God bestowed’
‘as those did who did not accept it’ made ‘siding with those who did not accept it’, closer to the plain dative and still flagged in the note
γόησιν clause recast as ‘the illusions that sorcerers display by deceiving the eyes’ (passive participle + dative of agent); note corrected to match
Checked John 5:39, Colossians 4:6, 1 Peter 3:15 (Origen’s ‘faith’ for ‘hope’ kept and noted)
